```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(tlmixture)
```

This example shows how to analyze data where observations are not
independent, e.g. siblings within families. It covers:

1. orthogonalizing exposures with family-aware cross-fitting,
2. running `tlmixture()` with and without cluster-robust standard errors, and
3. passing a customized mixture function so its internal cross-validation
   also keeps families together.

## Simulate clustered data

Families of 1 to 3 children. Siblings share a family effect on the outcome
and on the first exposure, so observations within a family are correlated.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(1, "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")

n_families = 400
family_size = sample(1:3, n_families, replace = TRUE)
family = rep(seq_len(n_families), family_size)
n = length(family)

family_effect = rnorm(n_families, sd = 1.5)[family]

df = data.frame(
  w1 = rnorm(n),
  w2 = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  family = family)

# Exposures depend on the covariates, and the first on the family as well.
df$a1 = 0.5 * df$w1 + rnorm(n_families)[family] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
df$a2 = 0.3 * df$w2 + rnorm(n)
df$a3 = rnorm(n)

df$y = 1 + 0.6 * df$a1 + 0.3 * df$a2 + 0.5 * df$w1 + family_effect + rnorm(n)

task = list(
  outcome = "y",
  exposures = c("a1", "a2", "a3"),
  covariates = c("w1", "w2"),
  id = "family")

cat("Children:", n, " Families:", n_families, "\n")
table(family_size)
```

## Orthogonalize exposures

As in the other analyses in this folder, each exposure is replaced by its
residual given the covariates, A' = A - E[A | W]. Here E[A | W] is estimated
nonparametrically with SuperLearner, combining a random forest (ranger) with
a glm. A forest on its own can leave some linear confounding behind (it
flattens smooth trends near the edges of the covariate range); the glm
captures those, and SuperLearner weights the two by cross-validated fit.

With clustered data the prediction for each child should come from a model
that never saw the child's family. Ranger's out-of-bag predictions do not
guarantee that (a tree can be trained on a sibling), so E[A | W] is
cross-fitted instead, over folds that keep whole families together, and
SuperLearner's own internal folds are grouped by family as well (`id`).

```{r orthogonalize}
library(SuperLearner)

# Assign whole families to folds.
n_folds = 5
families = unique(df[[task$id]])
family_fold = sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = length(families)))
fold = family_fold[match(df[[task$id]], families)]

# No family is split across folds.
stopifnot(all(tapply(fold, df[[task$id]], function(x) length(unique(x))) == 1))

df_ortho = df
for (exposure in task$exposures) {
  fitted = rep(NA_real_, n)
  for (k in seq_len(n_folds)) {
    train = fold != k
    # Estimate E[A | W] without fold k's families; SuperLearner's internal
    # CV also keeps families together.
    sl = SuperLearner(Y = df[[exposure]][train],
                      X = df[train, task$covariates, drop = FALSE],
                      newX = df[!train, task$covariates, drop = FALSE],
                      family = gaussian(),
                      SL.library = c("SL.mean", "SL.glm", "SL.ranger"),
                      id = df[[task$id]][train],
                      cvControl = list(V = 5))
    fitted[!train] = sl$SL.predict[, 1]
  }
  # A' = A - E[A | W]
  df_ortho[[exposure]] = df[[exposure]] - fitted
}

# The orthogonalized exposures are (nearly) uncorrelated with the covariates.
round(cor(df_ortho[, task$exposures], df_ortho[, task$covariates]), 3)
```

## Run tlmixture without and with clustering

The `family` column is named in `id`, so it is used for clustering only and
never as a confounder. Without `id` it would be treated as a covariate, so it
is dropped from the unclustered run.

```{r run_tlmixture}
df_no_id = df_ortho[, setdiff(names(df_ortho), task$id)]

set.seed(2, "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
result_independent =
  tlmixture(df_no_id,
            outcome = task$outcome,
            exposures = task$exposures,
            estimator_outcome = c("SL.mean", "SL.glm"),
            refit_mixtures = FALSE)

set.seed(2, "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
result_clustered =
  tlmixture(df_ortho,
            outcome = task$outcome,
            exposures = task$exposures,
            estimator_outcome = c("SL.mean", "SL.glm"),
            refit_mixtures = FALSE,
            id = task$id)

# Degrees of freedom for the t-based intervals: families - 1.
result_clustered$cluster_df
```

## Compare the results

Treating siblings as independent understates the uncertainty. The clustered
standard error accounts for the within-family correlation, so its confidence
interval is wider. The estimates can also differ slightly, because the CV-TMLE
folds are formed by family.

```{r compare}
cols = c("rd", "rd_se", "rd_ci_lower", "rd_ci_upper", "rd_pval")
comparison = rbind(
  independent = result_independent$combined$groups_df[1, cols],
  clustered = result_clustered$combined$groups_df[1, cols])
signif(comparison, 3)

cat("SE ratio (clustered / independent):",
    round(comparison["clustered", "rd_se"] / comparison["independent", "rd_se"], 2), "\n")
```

## Customizing the mixture function

To change a mixture function's settings, wrap it and forward the dots.
Forwarding the dots also passes the cluster ids through, so the mixture's
own cross-validation keeps families together too.

```{r custom_mixture, eval = requireNamespace("sl3", quietly = TRUE)}
library(sl3)

my_mixture = function(...) {
  mixture_score_sl3(
    ...,
    estimator_mixture = Lrnr_sl$new(
      learners = Stack$new(Lrnr_glm$new(), Lrnr_mean$new()),
      metalearner = Lrnr_nnls$new(convex = TRUE)))
}

set.seed(3, "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
result_custom =
  suppressWarnings(
    tlmixture(df_ortho,
              outcome = task$outcome,
              exposures = task$exposures,
              estimator_outcome = c("SL.mean", "SL.glm"),
              mixture_fn = my_mixture,
              refit_mixtures = FALSE,
              id = task$id))

signif(result_custom$combined$groups_df[1, cols], 3)
```
